V1.1

Sc-structures, sc-Banach spaces, sums and level shifts

restated
indexed family, not nested subspacesinjectivity of the inclusions a fieldonly one structure in finite dim. (V1.31)

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1, p. 6

An sc-structure on a Banach space $E$ is a decreasing sequence of Banach spaces $E = E_0 \supset E_1 \supset E_2 \supset \cdots$ such that (1) every inclusion $E_{m+1} \to E_m$ is compact and (2) $E_\infty = \bigcap_m E_m$ is dense in every $E_m$. A Banach space with an sc-structure is an sc-Banach space; points of $E_\infty$ are smooth, points of $E_m$ have regularity $m$. A finite-dimensional space has exactly one sc-structure, the constant one. A subset $A$ inherits the filtration $A_m = A \cap E_m$, and $A^k$ is $A_k$ with the filtration $(A^k)_m = A_{k+m}$. The direct sum $E \oplus F$ has levels $E_m \oplus F_m$.

Example 1.2, the weighted Sobolev spaces $H^{m,\delta_m}(\mathbb R \times S^1)$, is not formalized (G.1).

Proved in Lean

A scale is an indexed family of real Banach spaces $E_m$, $m \in \mathbb N$, with injective compact continuous linear inclusions $E_{m+1} \to E_m$; the composite $E_m \to E_0$ is written $\iota_m$, and $E_\infty \subseteq E_0$ is the subspace of points that lift to every level, $E_\infty \cap E_m$ its preimage in $E_m$. An sc-Banach space is a scale in which $E_\infty \cap E_m$ is dense in $E_m$ for every $m$; then the image of $E_{m+k}$ is dense in $E_m$. For a finite-dimensional space $V$ the constant family $E_m = V$ with identity inclusions is an sc-Banach space, all of whose points are smooth. For sc-Banach spaces $E$, $F$ the family $E_m \times F_m$ with the product inclusions is an sc-Banach space $E \oplus F$, whose smooth points are the pairs of smooth points; the family $E_{m+1}$ is an sc-Banach space $E^1$, with smooth points those of $E$ seen in $E_1$, and $E^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate. For $U \subseteq E_0$ the level set $U_m \subseteq E_m$ is the preimage of $U$ under $\iota_m$.

What differs

  • The text's $E_m$ are subsets of one space $E$; the formal scale is a family of separate Banach spaces with injective compact inclusions, and "$x \in E_m$" for $x \in E_0$ means $x \in \iota_m(E_m)$. The two pictures are equivalent, and nothing in Chapter 1 uses more than the family.
  • Injectivity of the inclusions, implicit in "$E_{m+1} \subset E_m$", is a field of the structure; continuity is part of being a compact operator in Mathlib's sense.
  • Condition (2) is taken exactly as stated, density of $E_\infty \cap E_m$ in every $E_m$. The weaker "$E_{m+1}$ is dense in $E_m$" is derived, not assumed.
  • That a finite-dimensional space has only the constant structure, and that the constant sequence on an infinite-dimensional space is not an sc-structure, are proved separately (V1.31).
V1.2

Sc-operators and sc-isomorphisms

restated
the level maps are the dataIsScOperator is the text's formcontinuity on the levels is automatic

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.3, p. 7

A linear map $T : E \to F$ between sc-Banach spaces is an sc-operator if $T(E_m) \subset F_m$ and the induced $T : E_m \to F_m$ is continuous for every $m$. A linear sc-isomorphism is a bijective sc-operator whose inverse is an sc-operator.

Proved in Lean

An sc-operator $T : E \to F$ is a family of continuous linear maps $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ commuting with the inclusions, $\iota^F_m \circ T_{m+1} = T_m \circ \iota^E_m$. The family is determined by its base map $T_0$, and a continuous linear $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ is an sc-operator when for every $m$ there is a continuous linear $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ with $\iota_m T_m = T_0 \iota_m$; the two notions correspond. Sc-operators compose and add, and map smooth points to smooth points. An sc-isomorphism is a family of continuous linear equivalences $E_m \simeq F_m$ commuting with the inclusions; its inverse and composites are sc-isomorphisms. A continuous linear $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ with $T_0(E_m) \subseteq F_m$ for every $m$ is an sc-operator (the continuity of $T_0 : E_m \to F_m$ is the closed graph theorem), and an sc-operator bijective on every level is an sc-isomorphism (the open mapping theorem).

What differs

  • In the family picture an sc-operator carries its level maps as data; the text's "one linear map $T$ mapping $E_m$ into $F_m$ continuously" is the predicate IsScOperator on the base map, and the two are interchangeable (ScOperator.isScOperator, IsScOperator.toScOperator).
  • An sc-isomorphism is given by level-wise continuous linear equivalences; that the inverse of a bijective sc-operator is continuous on each level (the open mapping theorem) is built into this definition, and proved separately (ScIso.ofBijective). Likewise the continuity of $T : E_m \to F_m$ asked by Definition 1.3 is automatic for a bounded $T_0$ that maps $E_m$ into $F_m$ (isScOperator_of_mapsTo, the closed graph theorem; Findings, Chapter 3, item 233). V1.3

Sc⁺-operators are sc-compact

as in the book
the first condition is the secondsc-compactness proved

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.4, p. 7

An sc-operator $S : E \to F$ is an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator if $S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$ and $S : E \to F^1$ is an sc-operator. Since the inclusion $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ is compact, an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator is sc-compact: $S : E_m \to F_m$ is compact for every $m$.

Proved in Lean

An $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator $E \to F$ is an sc-operator $E \to F^1$ into the level shift, i.e. a family of continuous linear maps $S_m : E_m \to F_{m+1}$ commuting with the inclusions. Composing with the inclusion $F^1 \to F$ (itself an sc-operator) gives the underlying sc-operator $E \to F$, whose level-$m$ map $E_m \to F_m$ is a compact operator for every $m$; in particular $S$ raises the level, $x \in \iota_m(E_m) \Rightarrow S_0x \in \iota_{m+1}(F_{m+1})$.

V1.4

Sc-subspaces, sc-complements, sc-splittings

restated
compactness of $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ automatictopological sum from IsCompl + closedness

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.5, p. 7

A subspace $F$ of an sc-Banach space $E$ is an sc-subspace if $F$ is closed and $F_m = F \cap E_m$ defines an sc-structure on $F$. An sc-subspace $F$ has an sc-complement if there is an algebraic complement $G$ such that $G_m = G \cap E_m$ is an sc-structure on $G$ and $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$ is a topological direct sum on every level; $E = F \oplus G$ is then an sc-splitting.

Proved in Lean

For a subspace $A \subseteq E_0$ its level-$m$ part $A_m \subseteq E_m$ is the preimage of $A$ under $\iota_m$; it is closed when $A$ is. $A$ is an sc-subspace if $A$ is closed and, for every $m$, $A_m$ lies in the closure of $A_m \cap E_\infty$ (the smooth points of $A$ are dense in every level). A closed $A$ with the induced filtration is a scale, with the restricted inclusions compact, and an sc-subspace is an sc-Banach space with this filtration. $E = F \oplus G$ is an sc-splitting if $F$ and $G$ are sc-subspaces and $F_m$, $G_m$ are complementary subspaces of $E_m$ for every $m$; then $F_m$ is closed complemented in $E_m$ (the sum is topological), and the splitting is symmetric.

V1.5

Finite-dimensional sc-subspaces

as in the book
proof: a continuous projection onto $F$

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.6, p. 7

A finite-dimensional subspace $F$ of an sc-Banach space $E$ is an sc-subspace if and only if $F \subset E_\infty$. A finite-dimensional sc-subspace always has an sc-complement.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space and $F \subseteq E_0$ a finite-dimensional subspace. Then $F$ is an sc-subspace if and only if $F \le E_\infty$. If $F \le E_\infty$, there is a subspace $G \subseteq E_0$ with $E = F \oplus G$ an sc-splitting.

V1.6

Quotients of sc-Banach spaces

stronger
any closed $A$, not only sc-subspaces$(E/A)_\infty$ identified in V1.33

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.7, p. 8

If $E$ is an sc-Banach space and $A \subset E$ an sc-subspace, then $E/A$ with the filtration $E_m/A_m$ is an sc-Banach space, where $E_m/A_m = \{(x + A) \cap E_m : x \in E\}$.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space and $A \subseteq E_0$ a closed subspace. The family of quotient Banach spaces $E_m / A_m$, with the inclusions $E_{m+1}/A_{m+1} \to E_m/A_m$ induced by $\iota$, is an sc-Banach space $E/A$ (the induced maps are injective and compact, and the smooth points are dense on every level), and the quotient maps $E_m \to E_m/A_m$ form an sc-operator $E \to E/A$. As a statement: there are an sc-Banach space $Q$ and an sc-operator $q : E \to Q$ with every $q_m$ surjective and $\ker q_m = A_m$.

V1.7

Sc-Fredholm operators and their index

restated
(3) read as bijections $X_m \to Y_m$index independent of the splittingFredholm on every level

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.8, p. 9

An sc-operator $T : E \to F$ is sc-Fredholm if there are sc-splittings $E = K \oplus X$ and $F = C \oplus Y$ with (1) $K = \ker T$ finite-dimensional, (2) $C$ finite-dimensional and $Y = T(E)$, (3) $T : X \to Y$ an sc-isomorphism. Then $K \subset E_\infty$, $T(X_m) = Y_m$, $E_m = K \oplus X_m$ and $F = C \oplus T(E_m)$. The index is $\operatorname{ind}(T) = \dim K - \dim C$.

Proved in Lean

An sc-Fredholm splitting of an sc-operator $T : E \to F$ consists of subspaces $K, X \subseteq E_0$ and $C, Y \subseteq F_0$ with $E = K \oplus X$ and $F = C \oplus Y$ sc-splittings, $K = \ker T_0$, $Y = \operatorname{range} T_0$, $K$ and $C$ finite-dimensional, and $T_m$ a bijection of $X_m$ onto $Y_m$ for every $m$. $T$ is sc-Fredholm if it has such a splitting. Its index $\dim K - \dim C$ equals $\dim \ker T_0 - \dim(F_0/\operatorname{range} T_0)$, so it does not depend on the splitting. Consequences: $K \le E_\infty$; $\ker T_m = K_m$ and $\operatorname{range} T_m = Y_m$ on every level; and every $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ is a Fredholm operator in Mathlib's sense.

Sc-Fredholm operators are regularizing

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.9, p. 9

An sc-Fredholm operator $T : E \to F$ is regularizing: if $e \in E$ and $T(e) \in F_m$, then $e \in E_m$.

Proved in Lean

Let $T : E \to F$ be an sc-operator with an sc-Fredholm splitting, $e \in E_0$ and $m \in \mathbb N$. If $T_0 e \in \iota_m(F_m)$, then $e \in \iota_m(E_m)$. As a property: an sc-Fredholm operator is regularizing (ScOperator.IsRegularizing). Conversely, an sc-operator $T$ with $T_0$ Fredholm and $T$ regularizing is sc-Fredholm (V1.9); so $T$ is sc-Fredholm if and only if $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ is Fredholm and $T$ is regularizing.

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.10, p. 10 (proof §1.4.1, pp. 14–15)

Proved in Lean

Let $T : E \to F$ be an sc-Fredholm operator and $S : E \to F$ an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator. Then the sc-operator $T + S$ (with $S$ read as an sc-operator $E \to F$) is sc-Fredholm. Along the way: $T + S$ is regularizing, and every level map $(T+S)_m$ is a Fredholm operator. The construction is also proved as a criterion: an sc-operator that is Fredholm on level $0$ and regularizing is sc-Fredholm, and every level map is then Fredholm of the level-$0$ index.

V1.10

Partial quadrants and the tuples $(U, C, E)$

as in the book
closed and convex derived, not assumed$C^1$ a partial quadrant in $E^1$: V1.36

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.11, p. 10

A partial quadrant in an sc-Banach space $E$ is a closed convex subset $C \subset E$ such that there is an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ with $T(C) = [0,\infty)^n \oplus W$. One considers tuples $(U, C, E)$ with $U$ a relatively open subset of the partial quadrant $C$.

Proved in Lean

The quadrant of $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$ (with $\mathbb R^n$ carrying its constant structure) is, on every level, the set of $(a, w)$ with all $a_i \ge 0$; it is closed and convex with non-empty interior, and its level sets are the quadrants of the levels. $C \subseteq E_0$ is a partial quadrant if $C = T_0^{-1}(\text{quadrant})$ for some $n$, some sc-Banach space $W$ and some sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$. Then every level set $C_m$ is closed and convex with non-empty interior in $E_m$ and has unique differentiability at each of its points; the whole space is a partial quadrant ($n = 0$). $(U, C, E)$ is a tuple if $C$ is a partial quadrant and $U = O \cap C$ for an open $O \subseteq E_0$.

Sc⁰ maps

restated
total maps $E_0 \to F_0$target enters only as $f(U) \subseteq U'$the text's $V$ is $U'$

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.12, p. 10

For tuples $(U, C, E)$ and $(U', C', E')$, a map $f : U \to U'$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ (sc-continuous) if $f(U_m) \subset U'_m$ and the induced maps $f : U_m \to U'_m$ are continuous for all $m \ge 0$.

Proved in Lean

For $f : E_0 \to F_0$ the level map $f_m : E_m \to F_m$ sends $x$ to the unique $y$ with $\iota_m y = f(\iota_m x)$ when it exists (a junk value otherwise). $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U \subseteq E_0$ if for every $m$ and every $x \in U_m$, $f(\iota_m x) \in \iota_m(F_m)$, and $f_m$ is continuous on $U_m$. Then $f$ is continuous on $U$; if moreover $f(U) \subseteq V$ then $f_m(U_m) \subseteq V_m$; $\mathrm{sc}^0$ depends only on the values of $f$ on $U$, passes to subsets, and the composition of $\mathrm{sc}^0$ maps is $\mathrm{sc}^0$. The identity and every sc-operator are $\mathrm{sc}^0$, with level maps the $T_m$.

The tangent of a tuple

as in the book

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.13, p. 10

The tangent of $(U, C, E)$ is the tuple $T(U, C, E) = (TU, TC, TE)$ with $TU = U^1 \oplus E$, $TC = C^1 \oplus E$, $TE = E^1 \oplus E$. It is again a tuple: $TU$ is relatively open in the partial quadrant $TC$ of the sc-Banach space $TE$.

Proved in Lean

The tangent $TE$ of an sc-Banach space is $E^1 \oplus E$, the sc-Banach space with levels $E_{m+1} \times E_m$; for $U \subseteq E_0$, $TU \subseteq (TE)_0 = E_1 \times E_0$ is the set of $(x, h)$ with $x \in U_1$, and its level-$m$ part is $U_{m+1} \times E_m$. $TU$ is monotone in $U$. If $U$ is an sc-domain (open-in-convex levels with unique differentiability, V1.27) so is $TU$ in $TE$, and $T(U^1) = (TU)^1$.

V1.13

Sc¹ maps and the tangent map

hypotheses explicit
the family $Df$ is explicituniqueness of $Df(x)$ provedfinite dim. and compact-open: V1.34–V1.35not norm continuous: a $c_0$ example

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.14, pp. 10–11

$f : U \to U'$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ if (1) $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$; (2) for every $x \in U_1$ there is a bounded linear $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ with $|f(x+h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|_0 / |h|_1 \to 0$ as $|h|_1 \to 0$, $h \in E_1$, $x + h \in U_1$; (3) the tangent map $Tf : TU \to TU'$, $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$, is $\mathrm{sc}^0$. In general $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is not continuous into $\mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ with the operator norm, but it is with the compact-open topology; the $\mathrm{sc}^1$ maps between finite-dimensional spaces are the $C^1$ maps.

The text writes $Df(x)$ as if it were unique.

Proved in Lean

For a family $D : E_1 \to \mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ the tangent map $T_Df : TE \to TF$ is $(x, h) \mapsto (f_1(x), D(x)h)$. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $D$ if (1) $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$; (2) for every $x \in U_1$ the map $f \circ \iota_1 : E_1 \to F_0$ has derivative $D(x) \circ \iota_1$ at $x$ within $U_1$ (Mathlib's HasFDerivWithinAt); (3) $T_Df$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $TU$. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ if such a $D$ exists; scDeriv is a chosen one, and tangentMap the tangent map built from it. If $U_1$ has unique differentiability at $x \in U_1$, any two derivative families satisfying (2) agree at $x$ (the inclusion $E_1 \to E_0$ has dense range); on an sc-domain the chosen derivative therefore agrees with any admissible one on $U_1$, and the tangent map on $TU$. Being $\mathrm{sc}^1$ depends only on the values on $U$. Level $0$ of (3) says $(x, h) \mapsto D(x)h$ is continuous on $U_1 \times E_0$, and this gives uniform continuity of $D$ on compact subsets of $E_0$; for maps between finite-dimensional spaces on an open set, $\mathrm{sc}^1$ is $C^1$. The derivative need not be norm continuous: on $E = \mathbb R \oplus X$, with $X$ the sc-Banach space whose level $m$ consists of the sequences with $(k+1)^m x_k \to 0$, normed by $\sup_k (k+1)^m|x_k|$, the map $f(t, x)_k = \cos(kt)x_k$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ into $X$, and for every derivative family $D$ of $f$, $x \mapsto D(x)$ is not continuous on $E_1$ into $\mathcal L(E_0, X_0)$ with the operator norm.

  • The remark on the compact-open topology is formalized here as the uniform continuity of $x \mapsto Df(x)$ on compact sets of $E_0$, and as an equivalence with level $0$ of (3) in V1.34; the remark on finite dimensions is proved on open sets in Polyfold/Test.lean and on relatively open subsets of quadrants, with boundary, in V1.35. That $x \mapsto Df(x)$ need not be norm continuous is proved by an example, which the text does not give: $f(t, x)_k = \cos(kt)x_k$ on $\mathbb R \oplus X$, $X$ the weighted $c_0$ scale (the project's first infinite-dimensional sc-Banach space); the factor $k$ of the $t$-derivative is absorbed by one level, $(\pi/(n+1), 0) \to 0$ in $E_1$, but $\|Df(\pi/(n+1), 0) - Df(0, 0)\| \ge 2$, and the derivative is unique on $E_1$, so no derivative family is norm continuous (Findings, Chapter 1, follow-up item 1; formerly G.3). Updated in the third addendum of this page.
V1.14

Sc^k and sc-smooth maps

as in the book
$Tf$ built from the chosen derivative

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.15, p. 11 (unnumbered in the preprint)

Inductively, an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^2$ if it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and $Tf : TU \to TV$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$; then $T^2f = T(Tf)$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$, and $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^3$ if $T^2f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$, and so on. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^\infty$, or sc-smooth, if it is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ for all $k \ge 0$.

The preprint's numbered Remark 1.15 (partial cones) is not formalized; the inductive definition that precedes it is numbered 1.15 here, as the Lean files do.

Proved in Lean

$f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U$ by recursion on $k$: $\mathrm{sc}^0$ means $\mathrm{sc}^0$; $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ means $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with the tangent map $Tf$ (built from the chosen derivative) $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $TU \subseteq TE$. $f$ is sc-smooth if it is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ for every $k$. Then $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ implies $\mathrm{sc}^k$ (and $\mathrm{sc}^l$ for $l \le k$); $f$ is sc-smooth iff it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with sc-smooth tangent map; on an sc-domain, $\mathrm{sc}^k$ depends only on the values on $U$.

V1.15

Sc¹ in terms of the levels

restated
the extensions $Df(x)$ an explicit familytheir compatibility across levels provedon any sc-domain

HWZ §1.2, Proposition 1.16, p. 12

Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of $E$ and $F$ an sc-Banach space. An $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map $f : U \to F$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ if and only if (1) for every $m \ge 1$, $f : U_m \to F_{m-1}$ is $C^1$, so that $df : U_m \to \mathcal L(E_m, F_{m-1})$ is continuous; and (2) for every $m \ge 1$ and $x \in U_m$, $df(x)$ extends to a bounded $Df(x) : E_{m-1} \to F_{m-1}$ with $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ continuous on $U_m \oplus E_{m-1}$. In particular, at a smooth point $x \in U_\infty$ of an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map, $Df(x) : E \to F$ is an sc-operator.

Proved in Lean

Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$. Then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ if and only if there is a family of operators $D_m(x) \in \mathcal L(E_m, F_m)$, $x \in U_{m+1}$, such that for every $m$: $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is differentiable within $U_{m+1}$ at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with derivative $D_m(x) \circ \iota$, and $(x, h) \mapsto D_m(x)h$ is continuous on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$. For such a family, $x \mapsto D_m(x) \circ \iota$ is continuous $U_{m+1} \to \mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$ in the operator norm, so $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is $C^1$; and $\iota_m \circ D_m(x) = D_0(\iota x) \circ \iota_m$, so the $D_m(x)$ are the restrictions of one operator $Df(x) = D_0(x)$. For an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map with derivatives $Df$, the family is given by the level operators $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$ (V1.26). At a point $x \in U_1$ that is smooth, $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ is an sc-operator.

HWZ §1.2, Proposition 1.17, p. 12

Let $U$ and $V$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces and $f : U \to V$ an $\mathrm{sc}^k$ map. Then $f : U^1 \to V^1$ is also $\mathrm{sc}^k$.

HWZ §1.2, Proposition 1.18, p. 13

Let $U$ and $V$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces. If $f : U \to V$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$, then for every $m \ge 0$ the map $f : U_{m+k} \to V_m$ is of class $C^k$; moreover $f : U_{m+l} \to V_m$ is $C^l$ for every $0 \le l \le k$.

An sc-smooth map is $C^k$ from $U_{m+k}$ to $F_m$ for all $m$, $k$.

HWZ §1.2, Corollary 1.20, p. 13

Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of an sc-Banach space and $f : U \to \mathbb R^N$. If for some $k$ and all $0 \le l \le k$ the map $f : U_l \to \mathbb R^N$ is $C^{l+1}$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$.

If $f \circ \iota_l$ is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_l$ for every $l$, then $f$ is sc-smooth; if $f$ is $C^\infty$ within $U$, then $f$ is sc-smooth. The chain rule

as in the book
$W \subset Q \subset G$ plays no roleproved by the mean value inequalitysc^k and sc-smooth versions proved

HWZ §1.3, Theorem 1.21, p. 13 (proof §1.4.2, pp. 15–16)

Let $U \subset C \subset E$, $V \subset D \subset F$ and $W \subset Q \subset G$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces and $f : U \to V$, $g : V \to W$ be $\mathrm{sc}^1$. Then $g \circ f : U \to W$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$.

Remark 1.22: differentiability is guaranteed only with the loss of one level, yet the composition loses only one; the compactness of $E_{m+1} \to E_m$ saves the day.

Proved in Lean

Let $U \subseteq C \subseteq E$ and $V \subseteq D \subseteq F$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with $f(U) \subseteq V$, and $g$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $V$ (with values in any sc-Banach space $G$). Then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ on $TU$. With derivatives made explicit: if $g$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivatives $Dg$ and $f$ with derivatives $Df$, and $V_1$ is the intersection of an open and a convex set, then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivatives $x \mapsto Dg(f_1(x)) \circ Df(x)$; this existence part needs no hypothesis on $U$. Iterated: the composition of $\mathrm{sc}^k$ maps between sc-domains (in particular between relatively open subsets of partial quadrants) is $\mathrm{sc}^k$, and sc-smooth maps compose to sc-smooth maps.

The degeneracy index of a partial quadrant

as in the book
defined through a chosen presentationdefined on all of $E_0$ (junk off $C$)

HWZ §1.3, Definition 1.23, p. 14

Let $C$ be a partial quadrant in $E$ and $T : E \to \mathbb R^k \oplus W$ an sc-isomorphism with $T(C) = [0,\infty)^k \oplus W$. For $x \in C$ with $T(x) = (a_1, \dots, a_k, w)$ put $d_C(x) = \#\{i : a_i = 0\}$. The map $d_C : C \to \mathbb N_0$ is the degeneracy index; points with $d_C = 0$ are interior, with $d_C = 1$ boundary points, with $d_C \ge 2$ corners.

Proved in Lean

For $p = (a, w) \in \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ let $\#(p)$ be the number of indices $i$ with $a_i = 0$, and for a presentation $T : E \cong \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ of a partial quadrant let $d_T(x) = \#(T_0 x)$. The degeneracy index $d_C(x)$ of $x \in E_0$ is $d_T(x)$ for an arbitrarily chosen presentation $T$ of $C$ (and $0$ if $C$ is not a partial quadrant); by Lemma 1.24 it equals $d_T(x)$ for every presentation $T$ and every $x \in C$. On the quadrant $[0,\infty)^n \oplus W$ itself, $d(p) = \#(p)$.

HWZ §1.3, Theorem 1.25, p. 14

Given tuples $(U, C, E)$ and $(U', C', E')$ and a germ $f : (U, x) \to (U', x')$ of a local sc-diffeomorphism with $x' = f(x)$, then $d_C(x) = d_{C'}(f(x))$. Let $U \subseteq C \subseteq E$ and $U' \subseteq C' \subseteq E'$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, $f : E_0 \to E'_0$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with $f(U) \subseteq U'$, $g : E'_0 \to E_0$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U'$ with $g(U') \subseteq U$, $g \circ f = \mathrm{id}$ on $U$ and $f \circ g = \mathrm{id}$ on $U'$. Then $d_C(x) = d_{C'}(f(x))$ for every $x \in U$. At points $x \in U_1$ this is proved directly; a general $x \in U$ is approximated by level-$1$ points of $U$ with the same index, and $d_{C'}$ is upper semicontinuous.

V1.24

Fredholm operators between Banach spaces, and Riesz–Schauder

not in the book
Mathlib v4.33.1 has no Riesz–Schauderfinite codimension via Riesz's lemma

HWZ §1.4.1, p. 14 (quoted as classical)

The proof of Proposition 1.10 opens with "since $S : E_m \to F_m$ is compact for every level, the operator $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm for every $m$", and later uses that the image of a Fredholm operator is closed. The classical theory of Fredholm operators and compact perturbations is taken for granted.

Proved in Lean

For real Banach spaces $E$, $F$: a continuous linear map with closed range is a strict map (open mapping theorem), and one with finite-dimensional kernel, closed range and range of finite codimension is Fredholm in Mathlib's sense (the remaining conditions, strictness and complementedness of the kernel, are automatic). A finite-rank operator is compact. Riesz–Schauder: for a compact operator $c$ on $E$, $1 + c$ has finite-dimensional kernel, closed range and range of finite codimension, hence is Fredholm.

The compact-open lemma and the level operators $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$

not in the book
replaces the 2010 paper's $\Gamma(x)$Bochner integral formed in $F_m$

HWZ 2010 paper, Propositions 2.1–2.3 (the compactness argument) · p. 12

The proofs of Propositions 1.16–1.18 in the 2010 paper rest on one argument: for unit vectors $h_n$ of $E_{m+1}$ a subsequence converges in $E_m$ (compactness of the inclusion), so the continuity of $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$ gives the continuity of $x \mapsto Df(x)$ into $\mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$; and on the integral identity $f(x + h) - f(x) = \int_0^1 Df(x + \tau h)h\,d\tau$.

Proved in Lean

Compact-open lemma. Let $s \subseteq X$ be the intersection of an open and a convex set with unique differentiability at each point, $\iota : Y' \to Y$ a compact operator and $A : X \to \mathcal L(Y, Z)$ with $(x, y) \mapsto A(x)y$ of class $C^k$ on $s \times Y$. Then $x \mapsto A(x) \circ \iota$ is $C^k$ on $s$ into $\mathcal L(Y', Z)$; for $k = 0$, continuity on $s \times Y$ suffices and no hypothesis on $s$ is needed. Level operators. For an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map with derivatives $Df$ and $x \in U_{m+1}$ there is a unique continuous linear $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$ with $\iota_m \circ Df(x) = Df(\iota x) \circ \iota_m$ (the second component of the level-$m$ tangent map); $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ is continuous on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$, $x \mapsto Df(x) \circ \iota$ is continuous $U_{m+1} \to \mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$, and on an sc-domain $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is differentiable within $U_{m+1}$ with derivative $Df(x) \circ \iota$, hence $C^1$; if $f_m : U_m \to F_m$ is differentiable at $x$ its derivative is $Df(x)$.

The Fredholm index and its invariance under compact perturbations

not in the book
not in Mathlibadditivity under compositionhomotopy $u + tk$, not Kato's proof

HWZ §1.4.1, p. 14 (quoted as classical)

Not stated. The proof of Proposition 1.10 uses that $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm; that its index is that of $T$ is the classical invariance of the index under compact perturbations, which the text does not invoke.

Proved in Lean

For a linear map $u$ over a field, $\operatorname{ind}(u) = \dim\ker u - \dim(F/\operatorname{range}u)$; if $u$, $v$ have finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel, so has $v \circ u$ and $\operatorname{ind}(v\circ u) = \operatorname{ind}(u) + \operatorname{ind}(v)$; a bijection plus a finite-rank map, in particular $1$ plus a finite-rank map, has index $0$. For real Banach spaces, a Fredholm operator has finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel; if $v$ is a quasi-inverse of $u$ ($vu - 1$, $uv - 1$ of finite rank) and $\|v\|\|s\| < 1$, then $u + s$ has finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel and $\operatorname{ind}(u + s) = \operatorname{ind}(u)$; if $u$ is Fredholm and $k$ compact, $\operatorname{ind}(u + k) = \operatorname{ind}(u)$.

Sc-splittings are sc-projections

hypotheses explicit
used, not stated, in the text$\ker P$ for $(1 - P)(E)$

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.5 and the proof of Proposition 1.6, pp. 7–8

An sc-splitting $E = F \oplus G$ is a topological direct sum $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$ on every level. In the proof of Proposition 1.6: the map $P$ with $P \circ P = P$, continuous on every $E_m$, "is a sc-projection", and $G := (1 - P)(E)$ is then an sc-complement.

Proved in Lean

If $E = A \oplus B$ is an sc-splitting, the projections of $E_m$ onto $A_m$ along $B_m$ are continuous and form an sc-operator $P$ with $P_m^2 = P_m$, $P_m(E_m) = A_m$ and $\ker P_m = B_m$ for every $m$. Conversely, if $P : E \to E$ is an sc-operator with $P_0^2 = P_0$, then $P_m^2 = P_m$ and $P(E)_m = P_m(E_m)$ for every $m$, and $E = P(E) \oplus \ker P$ is an sc-splitting. So $E = A \oplus B$ is an sc-splitting iff there is an sc-operator $P$ with $P^2 = P$, $P(E) = A$, $\ker P = B$.

The smooth points of a quotient

Continuity of $Df$ for the compact-open topology

compact-open = uniform on compactaan equivalence with level $0$ of (3)the negative remark: an example (V1.13)

HWZ §1.1, after Definition 1.14, p. 11

Proved in Lean

Let $X$ be a metric space, $Y$, $Z$ real normed spaces, $s \subseteq X$ and $A : X \to \mathcal L(Y, Z)$. Then $(x, h) \mapsto A(x)h$ is continuous on $s \times Y$ if and only if, for every $x \in s$, every compact $K \subseteq Y$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, $\|A(x')w - A(x)w\| < \varepsilon$ for all $w \in K$ and all $x' \in s$ near $x$. In particular, for $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $Df$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is continuous on $U_1$ in this sense. The negative half holds by an example (V1.13): there is an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map $f$ on a relatively open $U$ in a partial quadrant such that, for every derivative family $D$ of $f$, $x \mapsto D(x)$ is not continuous on $U_1$ into $\mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ with the operator norm.

V1.37

The derivative tower: one $d^jf(x)$ on all levels

not in the book
the text's tacit identification, provedchain rule with the inclusions

HWZ 2010 paper, Proposition 2.4, pp. 51–53 (the derivatives $d^jf(x)$)

The proof of Proposition 1.19 in the 2010 paper writes $d^jf(x)$ for the $j$-th derivative of $f$ on whichever level pair $U_{m+l} \to F_m$ the argument needs, with one symbol for all of them: the derivatives taken with a finer domain level or a coarser target level are tacitly identified.

Proved in Lean

A derivative tower of order $k + 1$ for $f : E_0 \to F_0$ on $U$ consists of base-level maps $\Phi_i(x)(h_1, \dots, h_i)$ with $\Phi_0 = f$ and, for $x \in U_{m+l}$, continuous $i$-linear maps $\Psi_{i,m,l}(x)$ on $E_{m+l}$ with values in $F_m$ ($i \le l + 1$, $i \le k + 1$) such that: $\Psi_{i,m,l}(x)(h)$ seen in $F_0$ is $\Phi_i$ at the images of $x$ and $h$ in $E_0$; $\Psi_{i,m,l}$ is continuous on $U_{m+l}$; and for $i \le l$, $i \le k$ it is differentiable within $U_{m+l}$ with derivative $\xi \mapsto \Psi_{i+1,m,l}(x)(\xi, \cdot)$. If $U$ is an sc-domain, $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ and $f : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_{m+l}$ for all $m$ and $l \le k$, then the iterated derivatives within the level sets form a derivative tower of order $k + 1$. Two values of a tower with the same images in $E_0$ agree.

V1.38

Elementary maps and the induction $(\mathrm S_k)$

not in the book
induction on $s$ over all elementary mapsthe bound $n_i \le k$ not neededslots are sc-operators $X \to E^n$

HWZ 2010 paper, Proposition 2.4, pp. 51–53 (the statement $(\mathrm S_k)$)

$(\mathrm S_k)$: if $f : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^{l+1}$ for all $m \ge 0$ and $0 \le l \le k$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$, and every component $\pi \circ T^{k+1}f : T^{k+1}U \to F^l$ is a linear combination of maps $\Gamma : U^{k+1} \oplus E^{n_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus E^{n_j} \to F^l$, $\Gamma(x, h_1, \dots, h_j) = d^jf(x)(h_1, \dots, h_j)$, with $j + l - 1 \le n_i \le k$. Each such $\Gamma$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivative $d^{j+1}f(x)(\delta x, h) + \sum_i d^jf(x)(h_1, \dots, \delta h_i, \dots, h_j)$, and the components of $T^{k+2}f$ are again of this form.

Proved in Lean

Elementary data on an sc-Banach space $X$: an sc-operator $\pi_0 : X \to E^p$ (the base point), sc-operators $\pi_a : X \to E^{n_a}$, $a = 1, \dots, i$ (the vectors), and a target shift $m$; the elementary map is $z \mapsto d^if(\pi_0 z)(\pi_1 z, \dots, \pi_i z) : X \to F^m$ on $\pi_0^{-1}(U_p)$, with $d^if$ from a derivative tower of order $k + 1$ (V1.37). Under the conditions $m + i \le p$, $m + i \le n_a + 1$ and $i \le k$: the elementary map is $\mathrm{sc}^0$; it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$, by the level criterion of Proposition 1.16 (V1.15), with derivative $(\delta z) \mapsto d^{i+1}f(\pi_0 z)(\pi_0\delta z, \pi z) + \sum_a d^if(\pi_0 z)(\pi z \text{ with } \pi_a z := \pi_a\delta z)$; on $TX$ its tangent map is the pair of an elementary map of type $(p + 1, m + 1; n_a + 1)$ and the sum of an elementary map with $i + 1$ vectors and $i$ elementary maps with $i$ vectors, all satisfying the conditions (the one with $i + 1$ vectors provided $i + 1 \le k$). Hence, if the domain $\pi_0^{-1}(U_p)$ is an sc-domain and $i + s \le k + 1$, the elementary map is $\mathrm{sc}^s$. The shifts $E^p$ have $(E^p)_l = E_{p+l}$, with $E \cong E^0$ and $(E^p)^1 \cong E^{p+1}$.

What differs

  • The 2010 paper's $(\mathrm S_k)$ describes the components of $T^{k+1}f$; the formal induction runs instead on $s$, over all elementary maps on all sc-Banach spaces $X$ at once: an elementary map is $\mathrm{sc}^{s+1}$ because it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and its tangent map is the pair of an elementary map and a sum of elementary maps, all $\mathrm{sc}^s$ by the induction hypothesis. Proposition 1.19 (V1.18) is the case $i = 0$, $p = m = 0$, $X = E$. The text's $\Gamma$ is the case $X = E^{k+1} \oplus E^{n_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus E^{n_j}$ with the projections as $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots, \pi_j$.
  • The index conditions are $m + i \le p$ (the text's $j + l \le k + 1$, which the text derives from its bounds), $m + i \le n_a + 1$ (the text's $j + l - 1 \le n_i$) and $i \le k$; the upper bound $n_i \le k$ of $(\mathrm S_k)$ plays no role. That the new indices satisfy the conditions ("one checks" in the 2010 paper) is checked for each of the three kinds of terms.
  • The sums in the tangent map are handled by the sum rule for $\mathrm{sc}^k$ maps and the Leibniz rule by the derivative of the multilinear evaluation (V1.39).
V1.39

Sums of sc^k maps; the derivative of multilinear evaluation

not in the book
sum = addition after the pairingLeibniz rule for $(A, h) \mapsto A h$

HWZ 2010 paper, Proposition 2.4, pp. 52–53 (the terms of $T^{k+1}f$ and the derivative (11))

The proof of Proposition 1.19 in the 2010 paper shows that $T^{k+1}f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ by showing that "any of the terms" of its components is, i.e. uses that a sum of $\mathrm{sc}^1$ maps is $\mathrm{sc}^1$; and it obtains the derivative (11) of $(x, h_1, \dots, h_j) \mapsto d^jf(x)(h_1, \dots, h_j)$ by the product rule, without stating either.

Proved in Lean

On an sc-domain, the constant map $0$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$, the sum of two $\mathrm{sc}^k$ maps is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ and so is any finite sum. The evaluation $(A, h) \mapsto A(h_1, \dots, h_n)$ of continuous multilinear maps is differentiable at every $(A, h)$ with derivative $(B, \eta) \mapsto B(h) + \sum_a A(h \text{ with } h_a := \eta_a)$.

V2.1

Sc-smooth retractions

as in the book
total map, values off $U$ ignored

HWZ §2.1, Definition 2.1, p. 18

For a tuple $(U, C, E)$, $U$ relatively open in the partial quadrant $C$ of $E$, an sc-smooth map $r : U \to U$ with $r \circ r = r$ is an sc-smooth retraction on $U$. After Definition 2.3: for $x \in U_1$ the chain rule gives $Dr(r(x)) \circ Dr(x) = Dr(x)$, so for $x \in O_1$, $Dr(x)$ is a projection.

Proved in Lean

An sc-smooth retraction on $C$ is a set $U \subseteq E_0$ relatively open in the partial quadrant $C$ and a map $r : E_0 \to E_0$ (only its values on $U$ matter) with $r(U) \subseteq U$, $r$ sc-smooth on $U$ and $r(r(x)) = r(x)$ for $x \in U$. Its retract is $O = r(U)$; $O \subseteq U$, $O$ is the fixed-point set of $r$ in $U$, and for $x \in O_1$ the derivative satisfies $Dr(x) \circ Dr(x) = Dr(x)$.

as in the book

HWZ §2.1, Definition 2.3, p. 18

A tuple $(O, C, E)$ is an sc-smooth retract if $O = r(U)$ for an sc-smooth retraction $r : U \to U$ on a relatively open subset $U$ of the partial quadrant $C$.

Proved in Lean

Proposition 2.4: the tangent of a retract does not depend on the retraction

as in the book
proved from $r(U) \subseteq r'(U')$

HWZ §2.1, Proposition 2.4, p. 19

If $r : U \to U$ and $r' : U' \to U'$ are sc-smooth retractions on relatively open subsets of $C$ with $r(U) = r'(U') = O$, then $Tr(TU) = Tr'(TU')$.

Proved in Lean

For sc-smooth retractions $r$ on $U$ and $r'$ on $U'$ (both relatively open in $C$) with the same retract, $Tr(TU) = Tr'(TU')$. More precisely, $r(U) \subseteq r'(U')$ already gives $r' \circ r = r$ on $U$ and $Tr(TU) \subseteq Tr'(TU')$. $TO = Tr(TU)$ is the fixed-point set of $Tr$ in $TU$.

Definition 2.5: the tangent $TO$ of a retract

as in the book
junk value $\emptyset$ off retracts

HWZ §2.1, Definition 2.5, p. 19

The tangent of $(O, C, E)$ is $T(O, C, E) = (TO, TC, TE)$ with $TC = C^1 \oplus E$, $TE = E^1 \oplus E$ and $TO := Tr(TU)$ for any retraction $r$ onto $O$; explicitly $TO = \{(r(x), Dr(x)h) : x \in U_1, h \in E\}$. Definition 2.17: for $x \in O_1$, $T_xO = p^{-1}(x)$, the image of the projection $Dr(x)$.

Proved in Lean

$TO \subseteq E_1 \times E_0$ is $Tr(TU)$ for a chosen retraction onto $O$, and equals $Tr'(TU')$ for every other one; $TO = \{(r(x), Dr(x)h) : x \in U_1, h \in E_0\}$, and for $x \in O_1$, $(x, h) \in TO$ iff $h \in Dr(x)(E_0)$. The fibre $T_xO = \{h : (x, h) \in TO\}$ is the range of $Dr(x)$, a closed subspace of $E_0$.

Proposition 2.6: sc-smoothness on a retract is independent of the retraction

hypotheses explicit
(3) needs $f(O) \subseteq O'$

HWZ §2.1, Proposition 2.6, p. 20

Let $f : O \to O'$ and $r : U \to U$, $s : V \to V$ two retractions onto $O$. (1) $f \circ r$ is sc-smooth iff $f \circ s$ is. (2) If so, $T(f \circ r) = T(f \circ s)$ on $TO$. (3) $T(f \circ r)$ maps $TO$ into $TO'$.

Proved in Lean

For retractions $r$, $s$ onto the same $O$: (1) if $f \circ r$ is sc-smooth on $U$ then $f \circ s$ is sc-smooth on $V$; (2) then $T(f \circ r) = T(f \circ s)$ on $Tr(TU)$; (3) if $f \circ r$ is sc-smooth and $f$ maps $O$ into the retract $O' = r'(U')$, then $T(f \circ r)$ maps $Tr(TU)$ into $Tr'(TU')$.

bundle structure not formalizedlocality of $Tf$ proved

$T$ is a functor $\mathcal R \to \mathcal R$: $(TO, TC, TE)$ is again a retract, $Tf : (TO, TC, TE) \to (TO', TC', TE')$, $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$, and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$. If $r$ is a retraction, $Tr : TU \to TU$ is a (bundle) retraction.

Definition 2.11: charts and their compatibility

restated
chart as a partial equivalence

HWZ §2.2, Definition 2.11, pp. 23–24

A chart around $x$ in a space $X$ is $(V, \varphi, (O, C, E))$ with $V$ an open neighbourhood of $x$, $(O, C, E)$ an sc-smooth retract and $\varphi : V \to O$ a homeomorphism. Two charts are sc-smoothly compatible if $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(V \cap V') \to \psi(V \cap V')$ and its inverse are sc-smooth (Definition 2.7); $\varphi(V \cap V')$ is a retract by Proposition 2.10(1).

Proved in Lean

A chart on $X$ is a local model $(O, C, E)$ and a partial equivalence $\varphi : X \rightharpoonup E_0$ with open source $V$, target $O$, continuous on $V$ with inverse continuous on $O$. The overlap $\varphi(V \cap V')$ is a retract; two charts are compatible if $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is sc-smooth from $(\varphi(V \cap V'), C, E)$ to $(\psi(V \cap V'), C', E')$ and $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ back. A chart is compatible with itself and with its restrictions; compatibility is local: two charts compatible with every chart of a family covering $V \cap V'$ are compatible.

Definition 2.17: tangent vectors in a chart

restated
equivalence relation provedtransport via the chain rule

HWZ §2.2, Definition 2.17, pp. 25–26

For $x \in O_1$, $T_xO = p^{-1}(x)$, the image of $Dr(x)$. Tuples $(x, V, \varphi, (O, C, E), h)$ with $x \in X_1$, $\varphi$ a chart around $x$ and $h \in T_{\varphi(x)}O$ are equivalent, $(x, \varphi, h) \sim (x', \psi, h')$, if $x = x'$ and $T(\varphi \circ \psi^{-1})(\psi(x))h' = h$.

Proved in Lean

A tangent tuple is $(x, \varphi, h)$ with $x \in X_1$, $\varphi$ a chart of the structure around $x$ and $(\varphi(x), h) \in TO$. Its transport to another chart $\psi$ around $x$ is $T(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(x), h)$, computed on the overlap retract; transporting to $\varphi$ itself does nothing, transports land in $TO'$ over $\psi(x)$, and transporting to $\psi$ and then to $\chi$ is transporting to $\chi$. Two tuples are equivalent if their points agree and the transport of the first to the chart of the second is the second; this is an equivalence relation.

The topology is generated by the sets $\{\alpha \in TV : T\varphi(\alpha) \in W\}$.

Proposition 2.21 (1), (2): the M-polyfold structure of a sub-M-polyfold

hypotheses explicit
subspace topology on $A$paracompactness: instance argument

HWZ §2.2, Proposition 2.21 (1), (2), pp. 28–30

A sub-M-polyfold $A$ has a natural M-polyfold structure for which (1) the inclusion $i : A \to X$ is sc-smooth and a homeomorphism onto its image; (2) for every sc-smooth retraction $r : V \to V$ with $r(V) = A \cap V$, $i^{-1} \circ r : V \to A$ is sc-smooth.

Proved in Lean

Let $A$ be a sub-M-polyfold with the subspace topology. For a chart $\varphi$ of $X$ and data $(V, r)$ at a point, $W = V \cap \operatorname{dom}\varphi \cap r^{-1}(V \cap \operatorname{dom}\varphi)$ is open with $r(W) \subseteq W$, $r(W) = W \cap A$; $\rho = \varphi \circ r \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is sc-smooth and idempotent on $\varphi(W)$, so $\varphi(W \cap A)$ is a retract and $(\varphi|_{W \cap A}, (\varphi(W \cap A), C, E))$ is a chart of $A$. Any two such charts are compatible; they form an atlas and make $A$ an M-polyfold. (1) $i$ is sc-smooth (a homeomorphism onto its image by the choice of topology). (2) For any data $(V, r)$, $i^{-1} \circ r$ is sc-smooth on $V$. $A$ is paracompact (V2.17); for closed $A$ this is elementary.

Proposition 2.24: $d_X$ is invariant under sc-diffeomorphism germs

HWZ §2.3, Proposition 2.24, p. 31

If $f : (U, x) \to (V, f(x))$ is a germ of sc-diffeomorphisms between M-polyfolds, then $d_X(x) = d_Y(f(x))$.

Proved in Lean

V2.33

Remark 2.28: $T^R_xO \subseteq C_xO \subseteq T_xO$

stronger
the negative claim is false (proved)partial quadrant without tamenessFlor's theorem, the needed case

HWZ §2.3, Remark 2.28, p. 33

$T^R_xO \subset C_xO \subset T_xO$; naively one might expect $C_xO$ to be a partial quadrant in $T_xO$, which in general is not the case.

Proved in Lean

$T^R_xO \subseteq C_xO$, and $C_xO \subseteq T_xO$ by definition. The negative claim is false: at every smooth point $x$ of every sc-smooth retract (no tameness), $T_xO$ and $T^R_xO$ are sc-subspaces of $E$ and $C_xO$ is a partial quadrant in the sc-Banach space $T_xO$ (with the sc-structure induced from $E$), of dimension $\operatorname{rank} M = \dim(T_xO/T^R_xO) \le d_C(x)$, $M$ the matrix of $Dr(x)$ on $E/E_x \cong \mathbb R^{I(x)}$. The core is Flor's theorem in the needed case: for a nonnegative idempotent matrix $M$, the cone $\operatorname{range} M \cap [0, \infty)^\iota$ is generated by linearly independent columns of $M$.

What differs

  • The inclusions as in the text.
  • The remark's negative claim does not hold in our reading (checked in Lean). The remark asserts, without an example, that $C_xO$ is in general not a partial quadrant in $T_xO$; in our formalization it is one at every smooth point of every sc-smooth retract. $Dr(x)$ maps $C_x$ and $E_x$ into themselves, so $C_xO = Dr(x)(C_x)$, and modulo $T^R_xO$ it is the column cone of the nonnegative idempotent matrix $M$ of $Dr(x)$ on $E/E_x$; by Flor's theorem this cone is simplicial, and the sc-isomorphism $T_xO \cong \mathbb R^r \oplus T^R_xO$ of the proof of Theorem 2.31 carries $C_xO$ onto $[0, \infty)^r \oplus T^R_xO$. What can fail for a non-tame retract is only $r = d_C(x)$ (Theorem 2.31), which may well be what the remark means (Findings, Chapter 2, item 50; round-trip item V2.33, whose blind statement is proved false; formerly G.9).
  • The verdict “stronger” records that the positive statement is proved for every retract, where the text proves it for tame ones (Proposition 2.36, V2.42) and asserts that it fails in general; formerly “as in the book” for the inclusions alone. Updated in the third addendum of this page.

The sign arguments (the content of Lemma 2.29)

not in the book
replaces the path formulation

HWZ §2.3, proof of Lemma 2.29, pp. 33–35

For an sc-smooth path $\alpha$ in $O$ through $x$, the derivative of $\alpha_i \ge 0$ with $\alpha_i(0) = 0$ vanishes (two-sided paths) or is $\ge 0$ (one-sided paths); with $Dr(x)\dot\alpha(0) = \dot\alpha(0)$ this gives Lemma 2.29 (1), (2).

Proved in Lean

Let $f$ be sc¹ on $U$ (relatively open in $C$) with values in $C'$ and $x \in U_1$. Two-sided: for $v \in E_1 \cap E_x$, $Df(x)v \in E'_{f(x)}$, and by density $Df(x)(E_x) \subseteq E'_{f(x)}$. One-sided: for $v \in E_1 \cap C_x$, $Df(x)v \in C'_{f(x)}$, and $Df(x)(C_x) \subseteq C'_{f(x)}$. For a retraction, $Dr(x)E_x \subseteq E_x$ at every $x \in O_1$.

Proposition 2.30: invariance of $T^R_xO$ and $C_xO$

stronger
level-$1$ points, sc¹ germsnot via Lemma 2.29

HWZ §2.3, Proposition 2.30, p. 35

If $f : (O, x) \to (O', f(x))$ is a germ of sc-diffeomorphism between retracts, $x \in O_\infty$, then $Tf(x)T^R_xO = T^R_yO'$ and $Tf(x)C_xO = C_yO'$, $y = f(x)$.

Proved in Lean

Let $r$, $r'$ be retractions onto $O$, $O'$, and $F$, $G$ maps with $F \circ r$, $G \circ r'$ sc¹, $F(O) \subseteq O'$, $G(O') \subseteq O$, inverse to each other on $O$, $O'$ (a germ of sc-diffeomorphisms; every sc-smooth map between retracts with sc-smooth inverse is one). For $x \in O_1$ and $y = (F \circ r)(x)$, with $Tf(x) = D(F \circ r)(x)$: $Tf(x)(T^R_xO) = T^R_yO'$ and $Tf(x)(C_xO) = C_yO'$. Moreover $D(G \circ r')(y) \circ D(F \circ r)(x) = Dr(x)$, $D(F \circ r)(x) \circ D(G \circ r')(y) = Dr'(y)$.

Definition 2.34: tame retractions and tame retracts

restated
presentation-independent (proved)

HWZ §2.4, Definition 2.34, pp. 39–40

An sc-smooth retraction $r : U \to U$ is tame if (1) $d_C(r(x)) = d_C(x)$ on $U$ and (2) at every smooth $x \in O$ there is an sc-subspace $A \subset E_x$ with $E = T_xO \oplus A$. A tame retract is the image of a tame retraction.

Proved in Lean

$r$ is tame for the presentation $T$ if (1) $d_C(r(x)) = d_C(x)$ for $x \in U$ and (2) for every smooth $x \in O_1$ there is $A \le E_x$ with $E = Dr(x)E \oplus A$ an sc-splitting (both summands sc-subspaces, complementary on every level). $r$ is tame if it is tame for every presentation of $C$, equivalently for one; a tame retract is the retract of a tame retraction. The identity of a relatively open $U \subseteq C$ is tame, and restrictions of tame retractions to $U \cap r^{-1}(V)$, $V$ open, are tame.

HWZ §2.4, Definition 2.39, p. 43

A face of a tame M-polyfold is the closure of a connected component of $\{d_X = 1\}$; $X$ is face-structured if every $x$ lies in exactly $d_X(x)$ faces.

HWZ §2.4, Lemma 2.40, p. 43

For a tame retract $(O, C, E)$, the faces of $O$ are the connected components of the sets $f \cap O$, $f$ an extended face; the components of $f \cap O$ and $f' \cap O$ through $x$ agree iff $f = f'$.

For $x \in O$ with $\lambda_i(x) = 0$, if the components of $f_i \cap O$ and $f_j \cap O$ through $x$ coincide then $i = j$. These are the faces of the M-polyfold $O$.

Proposition 2.43: faces of a tame retract are tame sub-M-polyfolds

restated
tame model on $\mathbb R^k \oplus W$$U^*$ from balls and $P_i$-preimagesno hypothesis added

HWZ §2.4, Proposition 2.43, pp. 44–45

For a tame retraction $r$ onto $O$ and a face $F$ of $O$: there are an open neighbourhood $V^*$ of $F$ in $U$ and an sc-smooth retraction $s : V^* \to V^*$ onto $F$; $s$ restricted to $V = O \cap V^*$ makes $F$ a sub-M-polyfold of $O$. $F$ is tame and $d_F(x) = d_O(x) - 1$ for $x \in F$.

Proved in Lean

Let $r$ be tame for $T$ and $F$ a face of the retract, $F \subseteq f_i$. (a) There is an sc-smooth retraction $S$ on $U^* \subseteq U$, relatively open in $C$ with $F \subseteq U^*$, with retract $F$ and $S = r \circ P_i$, $P_i$ the sc-projection onto $f_i$; every face of the M-polyfold $O$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $O$. (b) With the sc-operators $\iota : \mathbb R^k \oplus W \to f_i$ (insert a zero coordinate) and $\pi : E \to \mathbb R^k \oplus W$ (delete it), $r' = \pi \circ r \circ \iota$ on $\iota^{-1}(U^*)$ is a tame retraction of $[0, \infty)^k \oplus W$ onto $\pi(F)$, and $d_{C'}(\pi y) + 1 = d_C(y)$ on $F$. (c) A face $F$ of a tame retract $O$, with its sub-M-polyfold structure, is a tame M-polyfold and $d_F(x) + 1 = d_O(x)$ for $x \in F$.

Proposition 2.44: local faces and their intersections are tame

restated
face germs = faces of a tame chart$d_A + \#\sigma = d_X$ on all of $A$corners at once, no induction

HWZ §2.4, Proposition 2.44, p. 46

In a tame M-polyfold every point $x$ has $d_X(x)$ local faces containing $x$; they are tame M-polyfolds with $d_F(x) = d_X(x) - 1$. The intersection $F^\sigma$ of the local faces of $\sigma \subseteq \mathcal F_x$ is a tame M-polyfold of codimension $\#\sigma$ with $d_{F^\sigma}(x) = d_X(x) - \#\sigma$ (stated without proof).

Proved in Lean

Let $X$ be tame and $x \in X$. There is a chart $\varphi : V \to O$ of the structure around $x$, with a tame retraction onto $O$, such that the point $\varphi(x)$ lies in exactly $d_X(x)$ faces of the M-polyfold $O$, and every face $F$ of $O$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $O$ which, with its induced structure, is tame, with $d_F(\varphi(x)) + 1 = d_X(x)$ when $\varphi(x) \in F$. For every set $\sigma$ of face germs at $x$, i.e. $\sigma \subseteq I(\varphi(x))$, there are pairwise distinct faces $F_i \ni \varphi(x)$ of the retract ($i \in \sigma$, $F_i$ in the $i$-th coordinate hyperplane) and an open $B \ni \varphi(x)$ such that $A = \{y \in V : \varphi(y) \in B,\ \varphi(y) \in F_i\ \forall i \in \sigma\}$ (whose germ at $x$ is $F^\sigma_x$) is a sub-M-polyfold of $X$, tame with its induced structure, and $d_A(y) + \#\sigma = d_X(y)$ for all $y \in A$.

Theorem 2.45: interiors of faces and faces of face-structured M-polyfolds

hypotheses explicit
"interior" = $F \cap \{d_X = 1\}$counting argument made explicit

HWZ §2.4, Theorem 2.45, p. 46

The interior of a face $F$ in a tame M-polyfold is an sc-smooth sub-M-polyfold of $X$. If $X$ is face-structured, every face is a sub-M-polyfold, its induced structure is tame, and $i : F \to X$ satisfies $d_X(i(x)) = d_F(x) + 1$. Every point has a neighbourhood $U$ in which each $y$ lies in exactly $d_X(y)$ faces of $U$; if $X$ is face-structured, each $x$ lies in exactly $d_X(x)$ faces of $X$ (stated without proof).

Proved in Lean

Let $X$ be tame, $G$ the connected component of $\{d_X = 1\}$ through a point, $F = \overline G$. (a) $F \cap \{d_X = 1\} = G$ (the interior of the face), and $G$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $X$. (b) If $X$ is face-structured, every face $F$ agrees near each of its points, in a tame chart, with a face of the model retract; $F$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $X$, tame with its induced structure, and $d_X(x) = d_F(x) + 1$ for $x \in F$. A local criterion: $A$ is a sub-M-polyfold if near each point $\varphi(A)$ agrees on an open set with an sc-smooth retract contained in $O$. The face counts of the theorem are Proposition 2.42 and the definition of face-structured.

HWZ §2.4, proof of Proposition 2.46, p. 47

The projections are sc-smooth and the pairing of sc-smooth maps is sc-smooth.

Proposition 2.46: fibred products

stronger
$d = d_Y$ (and $d_X = d_Y$) without tamenessinverse of $\pi_2$ corrected

HWZ §2.4, Proposition 2.46, pp. 46–47

For a local sc-diffeomorphism $f : X \to Z$ and an sc-smooth $g : Y \to Z$, $X {}_f\times_g Y$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $X \times Y$; if $Y$ is tame, so is the fibred product, with $d(x, y) = d_Y(y)$; with both maps local sc-diffeomorphisms and both spaces tame, $d = \frac12 d_{X \times Y} = d_X(x) = d_Y(y)$.

Proved in Lean

Let $f : X \to Z$ be a local sc-diffeomorphism (each point has an open neighbourhood mapped sc-diffeomorphically onto an open set) and $g : Y \to Z$ sc-smooth. The fibred product $\{(x, y) : f(x) = g(y)\}$ is closed in $X \times Y$, hence paracompact, and a sub-M-polyfold of $X \times Y$; $d_{X {}_f\times_g Y}(x, y) = d_Y(y)$; if $Y$ is tame, the fibred product is tame. If $g$ is also a local sc-diffeomorphism, $d_{X {}_f\times_g Y}(x, y) = d_X(x) = d_Y(y)$, and if moreover $X$ and $Y$ are tame, $2\,d_{X {}_f\times_g Y}(x, y) = d_{X \times Y}(x, y)$.

Definition 2.47: $U \triangleleft F$, strong bundle maps and retractions

restated
$[1]$ via shiftFiberisomorphisms not defined

HWZ §2.5, Definition 2.47, p. 48

$U \triangleleft F$ is $U \times F$ with the double filtration $U_m \oplus F_k$, $0 \le k \le m + 1$, and $(U \triangleleft F)[i]$ with levels $U_m \oplus F_{m+i}$. A strong bundle map $\Phi(u, h) = (\varphi(u), \Gamma(u, h))$, $\Gamma$ linear in $h$, preserves the double filtration and is sc-smooth $(U \triangleleft F)[i] \to (U' \triangleleft F')[i]$, $i = 0, 1$; a strong bundle retraction is one with $R \circ R = R$; $R(u, h) = (r(u), \Gamma(u, h))$ with $r$ an sc-smooth retraction.

Proved in Lean

$\Phi : E_0 \times F_0 \to E'_0 \times F'_0$ is a strong bundle map on $U \triangleleft F$ if it maps $U \times F$ into $U' \times F'$, its first component does not depend on $h$, its second is linear in $h$ for $u \in U$, it maps $U_m \oplus F_k$ into $U'_m \oplus F'_k$ for $k \le m + 1$, and it is sc-smooth on $U \times F_0$ for $E \oplus F$ and (through the lift of the fibre component to $F'_1$) on $U \times F_1$ for $E \oplus F^1$. A strong bundle retraction is one with $R \circ R = R$; its base $r(u) = R(u, 0)_1$ is an sc-smooth retraction on $U$, $\Gamma(u, \cdot)$ is a projection for $u \in O$, and $R$ is an sc-smooth retraction on $(U \triangleleft F)[0]$ and on $(U \triangleleft F)[1]$. $C \times F$ is a partial quadrant in $E \oplus F$ and $U \times F$ is relatively open in it.

Definition 2.50: strong bundle charts, compatibility, atlases

hypotheses explicit
$\varphi$ a chart of $X$$[1]$-transition condition statedequivalence relation; charts restrict

HWZ §2.5, Definition 2.50, pp. 51–52

For $P : Y \to X$ (Y paracompact Hausdorff, fibres Banachable), a strong bundle chart $(\Phi, P^{-1}(V), K, U \triangleleft F)$: $K = R(U \triangleleft F)$, $V$ open with a homeomorphism $\varphi : V \to O$, $\Phi : P^{-1}(V) \to K$ a homeomorphism covering $\varphi$, bounded linear on fibres. Charts are compatible if $(\Phi' \circ \Phi^{-1})[i]$ are sc-diffeomorphisms, $i = 0, 1$; atlases and their equivalence.

Proved in Lean

A strong bundle chart consists of a chart $\varphi$ of the M-polyfold $X$, an sc-Banach space $F$, a strong bundle retraction $R$ on a relatively open $U \subseteq C$ whose base retract is $O$, and a homeomorphism $\Phi : P^{-1}(V) \to K = R(U \times F_0)$ with $\Phi(y)_1 = \varphi(P(y))$, linear on each fibre $P^{-1}(x)$ (continuity on fibres follows). Two charts are compatible if $\Phi' \circ \Phi^{-1}$ and $\Phi \circ \Phi'^{-1}$ are sc-smooth between the overlap retracts on $[0]$ and, through the lift to $F_1$, on $[1]$, and map fibre components in $F_1$ to fibre components in $F'_1$. Atlases: pairwise compatible charts covering $Y$; equivalence: the union is an atlas. Equivalence of strong bundle atlases is an equivalence relation, and two atlases are equivalent iff every chart of one is compatible with every chart of the other; this rests on the locality of compatibility. A strong bundle chart restricts to every open $s \subseteq V$ (retraction domain $U \cap r^{-1}(W)$ for $\varphi(s) = O \cap W$, $K_s = \{(u, h) \in K \mid u \in \varphi(s)\}$, $\Phi$ unchanged), and restrictions of compatible charts are compatible.

Definition 2.51: strong bundles; $Y[0]$, $Y[1]$, $P[0]$, $P[1]$ and $Y_{m,k}$

restated
$Y[1]$ topologized by the charts $\Phi[1]$one chart decides $Y_{m,k}$charts depend only on the class

HWZ §2.5, Definition 2.51 and the remarks after it, p. 52

A strong bundle over $X$ is $P : Y \to X$ (continuous surjection, $Y$ paracompact Hausdorff) with an equivalence class of strong bundle atlases. The charts induce a double filtration $Y_{m,k}$ and M-polyfolds $Y[i]$, $Y[i]_m = Y_{m,m+i}$; $P[i] : Y[i] \to X$ are sc-smooth.

Proved in Lean

A strong bundle is a continuous surjection $P : Y \to X$ ($Y$ Hausdorff paracompact) with Banachable fibres and a strong bundle atlas. The charts $\Phi$ form an sc-smooth atlas of $Y$, making it the M-polyfold $Y[0]$, and $P[0] : Y[0] \to X$ is sc-smooth. $Y_{m,k}$ ($k \le m + 1$) is defined by $\Phi(y) \in E_m \times F_k$ in all charts around $y$, and one chart suffices. $Y[1]$ is the set $Y_{0,1}$ with the topology generated by the charts $\Phi[1] : y \mapsto (\Phi(y)_1, \Phi(y)_2$ lifted to $F_1)$; these charts, onto the retracts $K[1]$, are pairwise compatible, their transition maps being the $[1]$-transitions, and make $Y[1]$ an M-polyfold; $P[1] : Y[1] \to X$ is sc-smooth. The charts of the strong bundle (StrongBundle.IsChart: compatible with the atlas) are those of the maximal atlas, which is equivalent to the given one: a chart is one iff it belongs to some atlas of the class, any two are compatible, restrictions of charts are charts, and equivalent atlases have the same charts.

Definition 2.52: sections of a strong bundle

restated
sc⁺ chart by chart = sc-smooth into $Y[1]$

HWZ §2.5, Definition 2.52, p. 53

A section is $f : X \to Y$ with $P \circ f = 1_X$; sc-smooth if sc-smooth into $Y[0]$, sc⁺ if sc-smooth into $Y[1]$.

Proved in Lean

A section is $f$ with $P \circ f = \mathrm{id}$; it is sc-smooth if it is sc-smooth $X \to Y[0]$ (Definition 2.14); it is an sc⁺-section if in every strong bundle chart of the atlas its fibre values lie in $F_1$ and its representative $z \mapsto \Phi(f(\varphi^{-1}(z)))$, lifted to $E_0 \times F_1$, is sc-smooth from $O$ into $K[1]$. This holds iff $f$ is a section and $f = \iota \circ g$ for an sc-smooth $g : X \to Y[1]$, $\iota : Y[1] \to Y$ the inclusion.

Proposition 2.54: the pull-back of a strong bundle is a strong bundle

hypotheses explicit
paracompactness of $f^*Y$ provedatlas of all pulled-back charts

HWZ §2.5, Proposition 2.54, p. 53

$P_f : f^*Y \to Z$ carries a natural structure of a strong bundle over $Z$ (\"the easy proof is left to the reader\").

Proved in Lean

For a strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and an sc-smooth $f : Z \to X$: $f^*Y$ is paracompact (it is metrizable, $Z$ and $Y[0]$ being metrizable by Theorem 2.16), $P_f$ is a continuous surjection, its fibres $P_f^{-1}(z) \cong P^{-1}(f(z))$ are Banachable, and the pulled-back charts $\Phi_f(z, y) = (\psi(z), \mathrm{pr}_F\Phi(y))$, with the strong bundle retractions $R_g(w, h) = (r_Z(w), \Gamma(g(r_Z(w)), h))$, $g = \varphi \circ f \circ \psi^{-1}$, form a strong bundle atlas; so $P_f$ is a strong bundle with this atlas. Locally: $R_g$ is a strong bundle retraction with image $\{(w, h) : w \in O_Z, (g(w), h) \in K\}$; the transition maps of pulled-back charts are $(w, h) \mapsto (\psi_2\psi_1^{-1}(w), \mathrm{pr}_F(\Phi_2\Phi_1^{-1})(g_1(w), h))$, sc-smooth on $[0]$ and $[1]$.

Theorem 2.55: Smirnov's metrization theorem

stronger
proved, not quotedpull-back form

HWZ §2.6.2, Theorem 2.55, p. 56

A paracompact Hausdorff space in which every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood is metrizable (quoted from Smirnov).

Proved in Lean

A paracompact Hausdorff space in which every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood is metrizable. More generally: a space $Y$ with open metrizable $V_i$ and a locally finite family of continuous $\rho_i \ge 0$, $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq V_i$, not all zero at any point, is metrizable, with the metric $\sum_i |\rho_i(x) - \rho_i(y)| + \min(\rho_i(x), \rho_i(y)) \min(d_i(x, y), 1)$; and if $\pi : Y \to X$ is continuous into a paracompact Hausdorff $X$ and every point of $X$ has an open $U$ with $\pi^{-1}(U)$ metrizable, $Y$ is metrizable. Metrizable spaces are paracompact (Stone, from Mathlib).

Definition 3.1: sc-germs of neighbourhoods

restated
a germ is a fixed sequence of sets

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.1, p. 62

An sc-germ of neighbourhoods $\mathcal O(C, 0)$ around $0$ in a partial quadrant $C \subseteq E$ is a decreasing sequence $U_0 \supset U_1 \supset \cdots$ with $U_m$ a relatively open neighbourhood of $0$ in $C_m = C \cap E_m$; its tangent $T\mathcal O(C, 0)$ is $U_1 \oplus E_0 \supset U_2 \oplus E_1 \supset \cdots$. A relatively open $U \ni 0$ with $U_m = U \cap E_m$ is an example; \"the size of the sets $U_m$ does not matter\".

Proved in Lean

An ScNbhdGerm E C is a family of sets $U_m \subseteq E_m$, each of the form $O \cap C_m$ with $O$ open and $0 \in U_m$, nested along the inclusions $E_{m+1} \to E_m$. Its tangent germ has levels $U_{m+1} \times E_m$; ofSet is the text's example $U_m = U \cap E_m$. The theorems on germs ask $C$ to be quadrant-like (every $C_m$ convex with nonempty interior, $0 \in C$), which every partial quadrant is; then derivatives on $U_1$ are unique.

Definition 3.3: sc-smooth section germs

hypotheses explicit
chart compatible with the atlas

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.3, p. 63

An sc-smooth section germ $(f, x_0)$ of $P : Y \to X$ is a continuous section $f : V \to P^{-1}(V)$ near the smooth point $x_0$ such that in a strong bundle chart with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$ the principal part $\mathbf f$ of $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to K$ has $\mathbf f \circ r : \mathcal O(C, 0) \to F$ an sc-smooth germ.

Proved in Lean

StrongBundle.IsScSmoothSectionGerm f x₀: $x_0$ smooth, and for some strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas (StrongBundle.IsChart) with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$, $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$ (the text’s germ reading). An sc-smooth section is an sc-smooth section germ at every smooth point with a centred chart (with the germ $U \cap E_m$).

Before, it was required on the whole $U$ of the chart (levels $U \cap E_m$), which is stricter: a function $C^k$ on $(-1/k, 1/k)$ for every $k$ is an sc-smooth germ in the constant scale $\mathbb R$ and sc-smooth on no neighbourhood of $0$ (exists_isScSmoothGerm_not_isScSmooth). No theorem assumes the definition. Hence “hypotheses explicit” again (“narrower” from the third addendum until the fourth) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 260; round-trip item V3.5).

The section algebra and the sum rule

not in the book
not stated in the textfirst use of the [1]-compatibility

HWZ §3.1, used in Theorems 3.12, 3.15 ("$f + s$ is an sc-smooth section") · p. 71

Not stated: the fibrewise sum of sections, principal parts in a chart, the sum rule of the sc-calculus, and the sc-smoothness of the local representatives of sc$^+$-sections in a chart that is not in the atlas.

Proved in Lean

The fibrewise sum $f + s$ is a section with principal part $\mathbf f + \mathbf s$ in every chart; $f(x) = 0$ iff $\mathbf f(\varphi(x)) = 0$; the fibres of $K$ are linear. Sums, differences and negatives of sc-smooth maps on relatively open subsets of partial quadrants are sc-smooth. In every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas, $z \mapsto (z, \mathbf f(z))$ is sc-smooth $O \to K$ for an sc-smooth section and $z \mapsto (z, \mathbf s_1(z))$ is sc-smooth $O \to K[1]$ for an sc$^+$-section.

Definition 3.4: fillers

hypotheses explicit
sc¹ of the map in (3) requiredprincipal parts only

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.4, p. 64

For a tame strong local bundle $K = R(U \triangleleft F) \to O$, $R(u, h) = (r(u), \rho(u)h)$, $r(0) = 0$, an sc-smooth section germ $(f, 0)$ has a filling $(g, 0)$ (an sc-smooth section germ of $U \triangleleft F \to U$) if (1) $f = g$ on $O$ near $0$; (2) $g(y) = \rho(r(y))g(y)$ for $y \in U$ near $0$ forces $y \in O$; (3) the linearization of $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ at $0$, restricted to $\ker Dr(0)$, is a topological isomorphism onto $\ker\rho(0)$.

Proved in Lean

IsFillingGerm for the principal parts $f, g : E_0 \to F_0$ (the text’s germ reading, also Definition 3.6, V3.9): $g$ is an sc-smooth germ on an sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$; (1) and (2) near $0$; (3) the map $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ (fillDefect) is an sc$^1$-germ on $G$ with a derivative family $Dk$, and $Dk(0)$ induces a continuous linear equivalence $\ker Dr(0) \simeq \ker\rho(0)$. Here $r(u) = (R(u, 0))_1$, $\rho(u)h = (R(u, h))_2$, with $R(u, h) = (r(u), \rho(u)h)$, $r \circ r = r$, $\rho(x)$ a projection for $x \in O$, and $\rho(u)$ a bounded operator. The whole-chart form IsFillerOf asks the map in (3) to be sc$^1$ on all of $U$ and says nothing about the regularity of $g$.

Proposition 3.5: the filler and the linearization

stronger
index equality without finiteness$Tf(0)$ is $Dg(0)$ on $Dr(0)E$sc form: filler (3) on level 0 sufficessc converse needs (3) on every level

HWZ §3.1, the paragraph after Definition 3.4 and Proposition 3.5, pp. 64–65

If $f$ has the filling $g$ and $f(0) = 0$, then in the splittings $E = Dr(0)E \oplus \ker Dr(0)$, $F = \rho(0)F \oplus \ker\rho(0)$, $Dg(0) = \begin{pmatrix} Tf(0) & * \\ 0 & C \end{pmatrix}$ with $C$ an isomorphism, and (1) $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is; (2) $Tf(0)$ is Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, with equal index.

Proved in Lean

For a filler $g$ of $f$ with $g$ sc-smooth, $g(0) = 0$ and $f$ a section of $K \to O$: $D(\rho(r(\cdot))g)(0) = \rho(0)Dg(0)$, $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0)Dr(0) = 0$, $D(f \circ r)(0) = Dg(0)Dr(0)$; and $Tf(0) := Dg(0)|_{Dr(0)E} : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is, Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, and $\mathrm{ind}\,Tf(0) = \mathrm{ind}\,Dg(0)$. The linear algebra holds for any idempotents $p, q$ and $L$ with $(1 - q)Lp = 0$ and $(1 - q)L : \ker p \to \ker q$ a topological isomorphism. In sc form: if $Dg(0)$ is an sc-Fredholm sc-operator, then $Dr(0)E$, $\rho(0)F$, $\ker Dr(0)$ and $\ker\rho(0)$ are sc-subspaces, $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is sc-Fredholm, of index $\mathrm{ind}\,Dg(0)$ on every level, and $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0) : \ker Dr(0) \to \ker\rho(0)$ is an sc-isomorphism (condition (3) of the filler on every level). Conversely, for $Dg(0)$ an sc-operator: $Dg(0)$ is sc-Fredholm if and only if $Tf(0)$ is sc-Fredholm and condition (3) holds on every level. The same for a filling germ (V3.7), with $Dg(0)$ the value at $0$ of any derivative family of $g$ on any germ (IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5, IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc, IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc_iff).

What differs

  • The proof exhibits $\ker Tf(0) \simeq \ker Dg(0)$ and $\mathrm{coker}\,Tf(0) \simeq \mathrm{coker}\,Dg(0)$ directly instead of the text's factorization and additivity of the index, so the index equality holds as $\dim\ker - \dim\mathrm{coker}$ with no finiteness assumption; closedness of the ranges transfers through the continuous $y \mapsto y - LC^{-1}(1 - q)y$, which is where \"topological\" in (3) is used.
  • The text's \"by linearization at $y = 0$\" needs $(u, h) \mapsto \rho(u)h$ differentiable and $g(0) = 0$; the target \"$(1 - D\rho(0))F$\" is $(1 - \rho(0))F$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 47).
  • Proposition 3.5 (2) is a level-$0$ statement. Its sc form in the direction Proposition 3.52 uses (“$Dg(0)$ sc-Fredholm ⟹ $Tf(0)$ sc-Fredholm”) needs condition (3) of the filler on level $0$ only, as the text states it: the higher levels of $Tf(0)$ come from the regularity of $Dg(0)$ (IsScFredholm.restrict), and condition (3) on every level then follows at the zero. The converse in sc form needs condition (3) on every level as a hypothesis; with level $0$ only it fails (an example on a weighted $\ell^2$ with the shift, Findings, Chapter 3, item 238, not formalized). Nothing in the text uses the converse (Findings, Chapter 3, items 234, 237, 238). Updated in the third addendum of this page.
  • For filling germs (the text’s reading of Definition 3.4) the proofs are the same, with the derivative family of the fill defect in place of the derivative on $U$ (Findings, Chapter 3, items 272, 289, 314). Updated after the switch of Definition 3.11 to the text’s germ reading (phase 2).

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.6, p. 66

$(f, x_0)$ has a filling if in a strong bundle chart with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$ the section germ $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to K$ has a filling $g : U \to U \triangleleft F$ near $0$; $(g, 0)$ is a filled version.

Proved in Lean

IsFillingGerm fb g (V3.7): $g$ is an sc-smooth germ on an sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$, $G_0 \subseteq U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$, and fills the principal part $\mathbf f$ near $0$; the centred chart is that of Definition 3.11 (V3.13). The whole-chart form IsFilledVersion ($g$ sc-smooth on all of $U$, filling in the sense of IsFillerOf) is a filling (IsFilledVersion.isFillingGerm), and a filling sc-smooth on all of $U$ is a filled version (IsFillingGerm.isFilledVersion).

A basic germ is an sc-smooth germ $f : \mathcal O([0, \infty)^k \oplus \mathbb R^{n-k} \oplus W, 0) \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$ with $f(0) = 0$ and $P_W \circ f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ close enough to $(0, 0)$ on level $m$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$.

Lemma 3.9: the fibre derivative of $B$ is small

stronger
sc¹ sufficesevery $\varepsilon$, every level $m$

HWZ §3.1, Lemma 3.9, p. 67

For $B$ as in Definition 3.7, every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $m \ge 0$: $|D_2B(a, w)\zeta|_m \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_m$ for $\zeta \in W_m$ if $(a, w) \in E_{m+1}$ is close enough to $(0, 0)$ in $E_m$; in particular $D_2B(0, 0) = 0$.

Proved in Lean

Four formal forms: (a) on level $m$, for an sc$^1$-germ $B$ in the working form of a contraction germ, $\|D_2B(a, w)\|_{L(W_m)} \le \tfrac12$ at points $(a, w) \in U_{m+1}$ with $a \in N(m+1)$, $w \in O(m+1)$, $\iota w \in O(m)$; (b) $D_2B(0, 0) = 0$ for an sc$^1$ sc$^0$-contraction germ; (c) on level $0$ with arbitrary $\varepsilon$: $|D_2B(x)\zeta|_0 \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_0$ for $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$. (d) as stated: for $B$ an sc$^1$ sc$^0$-contraction germ on a quadrant-like $\widetilde C$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $m$ there is $r > 0$ with $|D_2B(x)\zeta|_m \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_m$ for $\zeta \in W_m$ at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with $|x|_m < r$.

Proposition 3.10: the linearization of a basic germ plus an sc$^+$-germ

stronger
second statement on every level $m$sc$^1$ suffices; $f(0) = 0$ not used

HWZ §3.1, Proposition 3.10, p. 68

If $f = h + s$ with $h$ a basic germ and $s$ an sc$^+$-germ, $f(0) = 0$, then $Df(0) : \mathbb R^n \oplus W \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$ is sc-Fredholm of index $n - N$; and for every $m$, $Df(a, w)$ on level $m$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$ for $(a, w) \in E_{m+1}$ small in $E_m$.

Proved in Lean

For a basic germ $h$, an $s$ sc$^1$ into $(\mathbb R^N \oplus W)^1$ and $f = h + s$ sc$^1$: $Df(0)$ is an sc-operator, sc-Fredholm of index $\dim P - \dim Q$; it is $T_0 + S$ with $T_0(\delta a, \delta w) = (0, \delta w)$ (sc-Fredholm of index $n - N$) and an sc$^+$-operator $S$ built level by level. For the data of Theorem 3.38 and $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$, $D(h + s)(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$. On every level (the second statement): for every $m$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with $|x|_m < \delta$ the level-$m$ operator $Df(x)_m : \mathbb R^n \oplus W_m \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W_m$ is Fredholm of index $\dim P - \dim Q$, for $\widetilde C$ quadrant-like (partial quadrants are); $f(0) = 0$ is not used.

$(f, x_0)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if it has a filled version $(g, 0)$ and a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$ such that $g - s$ is conjugated to a basic germ: a strong bundle isomorphism $\Psi : U \triangleleft F \to U' \triangleleft F'$ covering an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi$ with $\Psi \circ (g - s) \circ \psi^{-1}$ a basic germ.

stronger

HWZ §3.1, Theorem 3.12, p. 70 ("an immediate consequence of Theorem 3.40")

Let $f$ be an sc-smooth section of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and $(f, x_0)$ an sc-Fredholm germ with $f(x_0) = 0$. There are nested open neighbourhoods $O(0) \supset O(1) \supset \cdots$ of $x_0$ in $X_0$ such that $\mathrm{cl}_{X_0}\{x \in O(i) \mid f(x) = 0\}$ is a compact subset of $X_i$.

A finite-dimensional sc-subspace $N \subseteq E$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$ if $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has an sc-complement $P$ (a good complement) with: for some $\varepsilon > 0$, $|p|_0 \le \varepsilon|n|_0$ implies ($n \in C \iff n + p \in C$). Definition 3.21 as written: IsScGoodComplement ($E = N \oplus P$ an sc-splitting, with the constant $\varepsilon$) and IsInGoodPositionSc; each implies the project's form. On a partial quadrant a smooth finite-dimensional $N$ in good position (algebraic complement) is in good position with an sc-complement, also inside any sc-subspace $T \supseteq N$; for smooth $N$ the text's good complements are the project's closed ones, and Definition 3.21 as written is the project's good position together with $N \subseteq E_\infty$.

Definition 3.28: sc$^0$-contraction germs and their working form

HWZ §3.3, Definition 3.28, p. 85

An sc$^0$-germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ if $f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ on level $m$ sufficiently close to $(0, 0)$.

Proved in Lean

IsSc0ContractionGerm C̃ G B: $B$ an sc$^0$-germ on $G$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, and for every $\varepsilon$, $m$ an $r > 0$ with the estimate for $a \in \widetilde C$, $|a| < r$, $|w|_m, |w'|_m < r$, these points lying in $U_m$. The working form ContractionGerm: the same data with explicit regions $N(m) \subseteq P$ open, $K(m) \subseteq O(m) \subseteq W_m$ ($K$ closed, $O$ open) on which $B_m(a, \cdot)$ is a $\tfrac12$-contraction ($O$) mapping $K$ into itself; every contraction germ has one.

Theorem 3.29: existence of the solution germ

hypotheses explicit
uniqueness region explicit

HWZ §3.3, Theorem 3.29, p. 86

An sc$^0$-contraction germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ admits a uniquely determined sc$^0$-solution germ $\delta : \mathcal O(\widetilde C, 0) \to (W, 0)$ with $f(a, \delta(a)) = 0$; proof by \"the parametrized version of Banach's fixed point theorem\".

Proved in Lean

In the working form, $\delta$ (the level-$0$ fixed point) is an sc$^0$-germ on $V_m = N(m) \cap \widetilde C$ with $\delta(0) = 0$, $(a, \delta_m(a)) \in U_m$ and $B(a, \delta(a)) = \delta(a)$, and every solution $w \in O(0)$ of $w = B(a, w)$, $a \in V_0$, equals $\delta(a)$. From Definition 3.28 directly: the same with uniqueness in a ball. The parametrized fixed point theorem: the fixed point of a family of $\tfrac12$-contractions of a closed set, continuous in the parameter pointwise, is continuous in the parameter.

Lemma 3.31: the contraction germ $f^{(1)}$

restated
regions unbounded in tangent directionsDefinition 3.28 for $f^{(1)}$ proved

HWZ §3.3, Lemma 3.31, pp. 86–87

If $f = w - B(a, w)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ of class sc$^k$, $k \ge 1$, with solution germ $\delta$ of class sc$^j$, then $f^{(1)}(v, b, u, w) = (u - B(v, u), w - DB(v, \delta(v))(b, w))$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ of class sc$^{\min(k-1, j)}$ with solution germ $T\delta$ (\"from the uniqueness\").

Proved in Lean

If $B$ is sc$^{k+1}$ and $\delta$ is sc$^j$ on $\mathrm{germ}(s) = (N(m+s) \cap \widetilde C)_m$, then $f^{(1)}$, in working form with parameter space $P \times P \supseteq \widetilde C \times P$, fibre $TW$ and regions $N(m+2+s) \times P$, $O(m+1) \times W_m$, $K(m+1) \times W_m$, is a contraction germ of class sc$^{\min(k, j)}$ whose solution germ is $T\delta(v, b) = (\delta(v), D\delta(v)b)$ on $(N(2+s) \cap \widetilde C) \times P$. Its map is $(\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ TB \circ \sigma, \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ TB \circ \Gamma)$ with $\sigma$ a reshuffle and $\Gamma(v, b, u, w) = ((v, \delta(v)), (b, w))$. If the working form also satisfies Definition 3.28 (as the one built from an sc$^0$-contraction germ does) and $B$ is sc$^1$, then $f^{(1)}$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ in the sense of Definition 3.28 on its germ, for every $s$: an $\varepsilon$-contraction near $0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ on every level.

Theorem 3.38: weak stability of basic germs

linear coordinate change$W$-component of $s$ only

HWZ §3.4, Theorem 3.38, p. 90 (proof pp. 90–93)

For a basic germ $f$ and the principal part $s$ of an sc$^+$-section with $s(0) = 0$ there is a strong bundle isomorphism $\Phi : U \triangleleft (\mathbb R^N \oplus W) \to U' \triangleleft (\mathbb R^{N'} \oplus W')$ covering an sc-diffeomorphism $\varphi$ such that $(\Phi_*(f + s))^1$ (levels raised by one) is a basic germ; $n - N = n' - N'$.

Proved in Lean

Given $f$ basic with contraction $B$ and the data StabilityData (the $W$-component $s$ of the sc$^+$-germ, $s(0) = 0$, and an sc-Fredholm splitting $W = C \oplus X = R \oplus Z$ of $1 + D_2s(0)$, which exists by Proposition 1.10): with the linear base change $\psi(a, w) = ((a, (1 - P_1)w), P_1w)$ and fibre change $\Psi(q, w) = ((q, (1 - P_2)w), L^{-1}P_2w)$, the germ $(\Phi_*(f + s))^1 = \Psi \circ (f + s)^1 \circ \psi^{-1}$ on $\psi(U_{m+1})$ is a basic germ with contraction $\hat B = L^{-1}P_2(B - S)$; zeros correspond under $\psi$; and $\dim C = \dim Z$.

Proposition 3.52: the linearization at a zero is Fredholm of index $n - N$

restated
sc-Fredholm, in every chartindex $n - N$ for every conjugation

HWZ §3.6, Proposition 3.52, p. 110

If $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and $f(x) = 0$, then $Tf(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is an sc-Fredholm operator (of the index $n - N$ of the basic germ, as the proof of Theorem 3.54 uses).

Proved in Lean

For a section $f$ with $(f, x_0)$ an sc-Fredholm germ and $f(x_0) = 0$: in the chart of Definition 3.11 centred at $x_0$, with the filling germ $g$ (a derivative family $Dg$ on a germ $G \subseteq U$) and the local sc$^+$-germ $s$, $Dg(0) : E \to F$ is an sc-Fredholm operator, $T_0O = Dr(0)E$ and $K_0 = \rho(0)F$ are sc-subspaces, and $Tf(x_0) = Dg(0)|_{T_0O} : T_0O \to K_0$ is an sc-Fredholm operator; for every conjugation of $g - s$ to a basic germ $h : O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$, $\widetilde C \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ (ConjugationData), both are Fredholm of index $n - N$ on every level. In particular $n - N$ does not depend on the conjugation. For an sc-Fredholm section the same holds in every strong bundle chart around a zero $y$: at the point $z$ over $y$, $T_zO = Dr(z)E$ and $K_z = \rho(z)F$ are sc-subspaces and $\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO \to K_z$ is sc-Fredholm, of index $n - N$ on every level.
